title: Given the heads of two singly linked lists, return the node at which the two lists intersect. If they do not intersect, return null. The intersection is by node identity, not by value, and the lists keep their original structure.
shortTitle: Intersection of Two Linked Lists — Length Diff or Two-Pass Alignment

s1_definition.profdef: Finding the intersection node of two singly linked lists is done by eliminating the length difference so both pointers reach the shared tail together. The elegant two-pointer method walks pointer A through list A then list B, and pointer B through list B then list A; they meet at the intersection node after at most one switch, giving O(n plus m) time and O(1) space.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Finding the intersection node of two singly linked lists is done by eliminating the length difference so both pointers reach the shared tail together. The elegant two-pointer method walks pointer A through list A then list B, and pointer B through list B then list A; they meet at the intersection node after at most one switch, giving O(n plus m) time and O(1) space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Two customers, Rajesh and Priya, each follow their own trail of linked statements, but at some point both trails merge into one shared trail of joint-account statements. To find exactly where they merge, each walks their own trail and then continues onto the other person's trail. Because both then cover the same total distance, they arrive at the shared merge point at the same moment.

**One line to remember:** Walk A-then-B and B-then-A; they meet at the intersection because both cover length A plus B.

sections.s2_technical:
Intersection here means the two lists literally share nodes from some point onward, like a Y shape. After the junction, both lists are the same chain. The challenge is that the two lists can have different lengths before the junction, so naive lockstep walking misaligns them.

The length-difference method is direct. Compute both lengths, advance the longer list's pointer by the difference so both pointers are equidistant from the junction, then walk both together comparing node identity with `pa == pb`. When they are equal, that node is the intersection.

The two-pointer switching method is slicker and needs no length computation. We set `Node pa = headA, pb = headB;` and loop `while (pa != pb) { pa = (pa == null) ? headB : pa.next; pb = (pb == null) ? headA : pb.next; }`. Pointer A travels list A then list B; pointer B travels list B then list A. Both traverse exactly lengthA plus lengthB nodes, so they land on the intersection at the same step. If there is no intersection, both become null at the same time and the loop exits with pa equal to pb equal to null, correctly returning null.

A senior-level nuance is that comparison must be by reference identity, not by value. Two separate nodes can hold the same value without being the intersection; only the same object counts. In Java this is `pa == pb`, not `pa.val == pb.val`.

Another nuance is why the switching trick terminates even with no intersection: after one full switch each pointer has walked lengthA plus lengthB, at which point both are null simultaneously, so there is no infinite loop. This is a common interview follow-up.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India links each customer's individual statement nodes into a chain, but when Rajesh (SAV2001) and Priya (CUR3001) open a joint account, both of their chains merge into a single shared chain of joint-account statements. Compliance needs to find the exact node where the two personal chains join the shared chain. This is precisely the linked-list intersection problem.

Problem 2 — The two personal chains have different lengths before the junction because Rajesh has more prior statements than Priya, so a naive side-by-side walk would never align. We use the two-pointer switching method that cancels the length difference automatically.

Problem 3 — The match must be by node identity, because two unrelated statements could coincidentally have the same amount; only the physically shared node is the true junction.

In the code: a `StatementNode` holds a statement id and a next pointer. An `IntersectionFinder` has a `findIntersection` method using the switching two-pointer technique. An `IntersectionDemo` main builds two chains that share a common tail and reports the junction node.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: Rajesh chain R1, R2, R3 then shared J1, J2 (length 5). Priya chain P1 then shared J1, J2 (length 3). The junction is J1.

Step 1: pa starts at R1, pb starts at P1. They are different, so advance.

Step 2: pa walks R1 to R2 to R3 to J1 to J2, then becomes null, then switches to headB P1. Meanwhile pb walks P1 to J1 to J2, then becomes null, then switches to headA R1.

Step 3: Now pa is at P1 (after its switch) and pb is at R1 (after its switch). They keep walking together: pa P1 to J1, pb R1 to R2, and so on, each having now traveled the length difference offset.

Step 4: Because both pointers cover exactly 5 plus 3 equals 8 nodes before meeting, they arrive at J1 at the same step. pa equals pb equals J1, loop exits, return J1.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26 22:05:00 [INFO] Finding where Rajesh and Priya statement chains merge into the joint chain
2026-10-26 22:05:00 [INFO] Intersection node found -> JOINT-1
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Rajesh: R1 -> R2 -> R3 ─┐
                          ├─► J1 -> J2   (shared tail)
  Priya:  P1 ─────────────┘
    │
    ▼ two-pointer switching (each walks A+B = 8 nodes)
  pa: R1 R2 R3 J1 J2 null→P1 J1
  pb: P1 J1 J2 null→R1 R2 R3 J1
    │
    ▼ pa == pb at J1
  Output: intersection node = JOINT-1
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the intersection node of two singly linked lists is about canceling the length difference so that two pointers arrive at the shared junction at the same instant. My preferred solution is the two-pointer switching technique, where pointer A walks list A and then continues onto list B, while pointer B walks list B and then continues onto list A. Because each pointer ends up traversing exactly the combined length of both lists, they are perfectly aligned and meet precisely at the intersection node. It runs in linear time with only constant extra space and needs no length computation at all.

A key property is that if the two lists do not intersect, both pointers become null at the same step after one full switch, so the loop exits cleanly with a null result and never loops forever. That is a classic follow-up question, and being able to explain why it terminates shows real understanding rather than memorization.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, each customer's statement nodes form a personal chain, and when Rajesh and Priya open a joint account their two chains merge into one shared chain of joint statements, forming a Y shape. Compliance needs the exact node where the personal chains join the shared chain, and this algorithm finds it even though Rajesh's chain is longer than Priya's.

The point I always emphasize is that intersection is by node identity, not by value. Two unrelated statements could coincidentally carry the same amount, so I compare with reference equality using the double-equals operator in Java, never by comparing the stored values, because only the physically shared node is the true junction.
